entries.title: Tre Jones playing every angle for Bulls, frustrating one big at a time
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — A smirk came across Tre Jones’ face when asked if there’s a time when he knows he’s got a guy.</p><p>That split second where the team’s opposing shot blocker thinks he’s about to make the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’</a> 6-foot-1 guard another victim only to quickly realize it’s instead going to be an “Oh (bleep)” moment for him.</p><p>Several Timberwolves players went through that at the start of this three-city road trip, including Rudy Gobert, and then in Cleveland Jones got 6-9 Thomas Jones twice.</p><p>Not only are there few Bulls players on the roster that are as quick as Jones, but even fewer that understand angles at the rim.</p><p>“He’s incredibly smart at attacking those angles; super-fast too,” coach Tiago Splitter said of his reserve point guard. “Finishing at the rim, reverses, you name it, all kinds of finishes. And also taking care of the ball. I think he’s been superb so far this season taking care of the ball and finding teammates.”</p><p>He has, but that’s not what frustrates opposing players. It’s Jones’ ability to use the rim or their own body against them, angling his body for baskets players his size aren’t supposed to get.</p><p>“I’d say it was always a strength of mine growing up but continuing to try and perfect it as I get older and older in this league,” Jones said of his rare skillset. “You see the different opportunities, different defenses, and just the difference of the professional game and college where college had a lot more guys in the paint, a lot more clogged, tougher to get all the way to the hoop.</p><p>“Here in the league guys can’t just camp out in the lane. There’s a different gravity that players generate because some guys can really score the ball, so using that to my advantage as well. When the rim is taken away, I’m able to make the right play and spray it out to those guys.”</p><p>As for that moment in a game when Jones knows a big is about to misread the situation and think he’s going to block him?</p><p>“Yeah, usually there’s a split second where I feel like I might have him in a tough spot where I don’t think he can recover,” he said with a smile. “So yeah, I usually have a pretty good idea.”</p><p></p><h3>Josh-ing around</h3><p></p><p>Fresh off a six-turnover game in Cleveland, Josh Giddey spent some time with Splitter watching film and trying to correct the ball security issue.</p><p>A problem the point guard wasn’t even trying to hide from. </p><p>“Sloppy with the ball against an active team, and it was on me,” Giddey said after that loss to the Cavs. “It was just bad from the start all around. Turnovers, defense, everything. I just want to put it in the trash and move on.”</p><p>Splitter came out of the film session feeling better.</p><p>“Just trying to help him try and see what’s going on in his mind, what he sees,” Splitter said. “The end of the day we’ve got to be more careful with the ball. Sometimes just play simple and make the easy pass, but I think he’s going to get better, bounce back.”</p><p>Maybe, but he did have two turnovers in the first five minutes against Brooklyn on Wednesday.</p><p></p><h3>Rising stock</h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Two-way contract guard Jaylin Sellers was named G League Player of the Week after averaging 26.6 points per game. Expect the Providence standout to move into the big-boy rotation at some point later this year. Splitter sure does.</p><p>“Helluva defender, he can shoot, he can be aggressive at the rim,” Splitter said of Sellers. “He’s doing what we’ve seen in the gym all summer. I love that kid. He’s going to be a part of our future for sure.”</p>

entries.title: Grant Taylor excited to join White Sox rotation that should see another addition
entries.summary: <p>With the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> shifting flamethrower Grant Taylor from relief ace to starting pitcher, it’s almost mandatory to draw parallels to a similar effort with Chris Sale 15 years prior.</p><p>After throwing 192 innings of 3.05 ERA-ball and making the first of what are now 10 All-Star appearances in what will almost certainly be a Hall of Fame career, Sale’s 2012 season is the archetype reliever conversion; both in terms of results and casting aside injury fears that once dogged his unusual delivery.</p><p>Yet, the Sox process with the 24-year-old Taylor will differ in some notable, ideally beneficial ways.</p><p>While arguing for his spot in the rotation with then-general manager Ken Williams eventually became part of Sale’s legend, Taylor touts a frictionless process where he made his wishes to start well-known, fulfilled the organization’s aims for a transition year in relief, and had an amiable conversation with GM Chris Getz confirming his role for 2027.</p><p>“They were all on board,” Taylor said Wednesday. “I want to help my team win and I think the game reflects that throwing more innings and doing it well helps your team win more often.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Grant Taylor innings are good, so more Grant Taylor innings should be more good. It's science. <a href="https://t.co/JXMYUUZ1Z7">pic.twitter.com/JXMYUUZ1Z7</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2123209971315749040?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Pitching alongside Jake Peavy’s last elite season and Jose Quintana’s breakout campaign, Sale powered a formidable trio in the first half of 2012. But when he (4.03 ERA after the All-Star break) and Quintana understandably ran out of gas late, the Sox’ lacking depth was exposed in a September collapse that handed the division title to Detroit.</p><p>After a 2026 postseason pitching plan that relied heavily on Taylor, Sean Burke, and off days, the Sox are hoping to build a deeper group. A source indicated to the Sun-Times the front office is looking to follow up this week’s agreement with Dustin May with another rotation addition of similar magnitude.</p><p>“A lot of guys are pumped up to get a guy like that,” Chase Meidroth said of May. “Facing him when he was with the Dodgers, my first year, he was unbelievable. He’s one of those arms you are happy he’s on your team.”</p><p>With Davis Martin, Noah Schultz, David Sandlin and others also gunning for rotation spots, the Sox hope to have the flexibility to rest Taylor as needed. And after battling injuries as a prospect, Taylor hopes to not require any breathers.</p><p>“Over the past few years I've built a pretty good team behind me,” Taylor said of his personal training staff. “I'm going to be relying on them a little bit more this year than I would in a typical offseason.”</p><h3>New assistant hitting coach</h3><p>Sources tell the Sun-Times the White Sox will hire Rays hitting coordinator Kyle Wilson to be their assistant hitting coach. Wilson will replace Joel McKeithan, who departed to become the Cardinals lead hitting coach.</p><h3>Leasure DFA’d</h3><p>With the signing of May becoming official, the Sox designated reliever Jordan Leasure for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster. Leasure will miss the 2027 season recovering from elbow surgery.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan
